title: Candy
description:
# Candy

There are `n` children standing in a line. The integer array `ratings` gives each child's rating.

Distribute candies using the fewest total candies while satisfying both rules:

*   Every child must receive at least one candy.
*   If a child has a higher rating than an adjacent child, the higher-rated child must receive more candies than that neighbor.

Equal ratings do not impose any ordering requirement.

## Example 1:

**Input:** ratings = [1,0,2]
**Output:** 5
**Explanation:** Give candies as `[2,1,2]`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** ratings = [1,2,2]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** Give candies as `[1,2,1]`. The last two children have equal ratings, so the third child does not need more candy than the second child.

## Constraints:

*   `n == ratings.length`
*   `1 <= n <= 2 * 10^4`
*   `0 <= ratings[i] <= 2 * 10^4`

tests.description: equal neighbors do not impose a greater-than rule
long rise followed by a drop needs a high peak
long down-slope after a peak is the classic slope pitfall
strictly decreasing ratings require the reverse staircase
all equal ratings only need one candy each
equal high plateau must not be treated as one rising slope
a later rise after a descent must restart cleanly

solutions.name: Two Pass Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Give every child one candy. A left-to-right pass enforces the rule against the left neighbor, and a right-to-left pass enforces the rule against the right neighbor while keeping the larger value from the first pass.

## Key Insight

The two neighbor constraints are directional. Once each direction is satisfied separately, taking the maximum candy count at every position satisfies both without adding unnecessary candy.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), for two linear passes and one sum.
- Space Complexity: O(n), for the candy array.
solutions.code: class Solution { public int candy(int[] ratings) { int n = ratings.length; int[] candies = new int[n]; java.util.Arrays.fill(candies, 1); for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { if (ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]) candies[i] = candies[i - 1] + 1; } for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) { if (ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]) candies[i] = Math.max(candies[i], candies[i + 1] + 1); } int total = 0; for (int candy : candies) total += candy; return total; } }

solutions.name: Single Pass Slope Counting
solutions.description:
## Approach

Read rating changes as increasing slopes, decreasing slopes, and flat breaks. Add the arithmetic-series contribution of each slope while tracking whether the peak already has enough candy for the descending side.

## Key Insight

A mountain of ratings needs candies `1..up+1` on the left side and `down..1` on the right side. The peak is shared, so it only needs one extra candy when the descending side becomes longer than the previous ascending side.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), with one scan over the ratings.
- Space Complexity: O(1), using only counters for current slopes.
solutions.code: class Solution { public int candy(int[] ratings) { int n = ratings.length; if (n <= 1) return n; int total = 1; int up = 0; int down = 0; int peak = 0; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { if (ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]) { up++; peak = up; down = 0; total += 1 + up; } else if (ratings[i] < ratings[i - 1]) { up = 0; down++; total += 1 + down - (down <= peak ? 1 : 0); } else { up = 0; down = 0; peak = 0; total += 1; } } return total; } }

solutions.name: Process Children by Rating
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort child indexes by rating from low to high. When processing a child, any lower-rated neighbor has already received its final candy count, so the current child can take one more than the maximum required by those lower neighbors.

## Key Insight

Constraints always point from lower rating to higher rating. Processing in rating order turns the local neighbor rules into a simple dynamic program over sorted indexes.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), dominated by sorting indexes.
- Space Complexity: O(n), for the order and candy arrays.
solutions.code: class Solution { public int candy(int[] ratings) { int n = ratings.length; Integer[] order = new Integer[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) order[i] = i; java.util.Arrays.sort(order, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(ratings[a], ratings[b])); int[] candies = new int[n]; java.util.Arrays.fill(candies, 1); for (int index : order) { if (index > 0 && ratings[index] > ratings[index - 1]) candies[index] = Math.max(candies[index], candies[index - 1] + 1); if (index + 1 < n && ratings[index] > ratings[index + 1]) candies[index] = Math.max(candies[index], candies[index + 1] + 1); } int total = 0; for (int candy : candies) total += candy; return total; } }

solutions.name: Lower Neighbor DFS Memoization
solutions.description:
## Approach

Define `candiesFor(i)` as the minimum candies child `i` needs after satisfying any lower-rated adjacent children. Recursively ask lower-rated neighbors for their candy counts, memoize the result, and sum all memoized values.

## Key Insight

The dependency graph is acyclic because every edge goes from a higher rating to a strictly lower rating. Equal ratings create no edge, so DFS with memoization computes each child's required candy count once.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each child checks at most two neighbors and is memoized once.
- Space Complexity: O(n), for memoization and recursion stack.
solutions.code: class Solution { public int candy(int[] ratings) { int[] memo = new int[ratings.length]; int total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < ratings.length; i++) total += candiesFor(i, ratings, memo); return total; } private int candiesFor(int index, int[] ratings, int[] memo) { if (memo[index] != 0) return memo[index]; int best = 1; if (index > 0 && ratings[index] > ratings[index - 1]) best = Math.max(best, candiesFor(index - 1, ratings, memo) + 1); if (index + 1 < ratings.length && ratings[index] > ratings[index + 1]) best = Math.max(best, candiesFor(index + 1, ratings, memo) + 1); memo[index] = best; return best; } }
